question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{76+4x}$ at the point where $x=-3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=76+4x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (4) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{76+4x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-3} & ={(\frac{2}{\sqrt{76+4x}})|}_{x=-3} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{76+4(-3)}} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{64}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Let $f(x)=\sqrt{-8x+41}.$ We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-8x+41.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-8.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-8) \\  & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{-8x+41}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{4}{\sqrt{-8x+41}}+3x^{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & =-\frac{8}{2\sqrt{-8(4)+41}}+3(4)^{2} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}+48 \\  & =\frac{140}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
